title: Haggerston to the Camera Obscura Wall: the Southern Sky, the Nested Shells, and the Comet That Came Back
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Haggerston, Shoreditch: the soap-maker's son
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, 8 November 1656, by Wikipedia and MacTutor. Old Style: England is ninety-six years short of adopting the Gregorian calendar, and every English date in this file before 1752 carries the same eleven-day offset.
stops.campa: A son is born at Haggerston in the parish of Shoreditch, outside the London wall, to a wealthy soap-maker and salter of the same name. Soap is a trade of ash and tallow rendered down; salt is the trade of keeping things from rotting. The father's money will buy telescopes and a passage to the South Atlantic before it runs out. The boy is given his father's name and will spend eighty-five years spelling it Edmond while the printers of two centuries set it Edmund. He is born under no comet. The one that will take his name is twenty-six years off.
suggested_refs: The parish registers of St Leonard's, Shoreditch, for November 1656
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Edmond Halley

stops.name: Pudding Lane, the Fire takes the father's money
stops.date_confidence: MacTutor attests the father's losses in the Great Fire to the year 1666 and dates them no further. 2 September is the first day of the Fire itself and is used as the sort key, not as a claim about when the accounts were reckoned.
stops.campa: The fire begins in a baker's house in Pudding Lane and runs for four days through a city built of timber and pitch. Eighty-seven parish churches and thirteen thousand houses go. The elder Halley holds property in the City and loses heavily. The son is nine. Twenty-one years from now that son will pay out of his own pocket to print the book explaining why the Moon does not fall, and will do it on a clerk's salary, having watched once already how quickly a fortune made in soap turns into ash.
suggested_refs: The Fire Court records of 1667, on City property losses
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Edmond Halley

stops.name: St Paul's Churchyard, captain of the school
stops.date_confidence: MacTutor puts the captaincy at about fifteen, which falls in 1671; the year is inferred from the age, and month and day default to 01 January. The death of his mother Anne is attested to 1672 by Wikipedia, without month or day, and is carried in this stop.
stops.campa: He goes to St Paul's School beside the burnt cathedral and is good at Greek and Latin and better at mathematics, and at about fifteen the school makes him its captain. He has instruments of his own by now, which is not what a soap-maker's son is expected to own, and he uses them on the sky over Shoreditch. In 1672 his mother Anne dies. The tradition that he was an astronomer before he was an undergraduate comes down through MacTutor with no document under it. What is documented is what he carried up to Oxford the following year.
suggested_refs: The registers of St Paul's School for the years after the Fire
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Edmond Halley

stops.name: The Queen's College, Oxford: the undergraduate with his own glasses
stops.date_confidence: attested to July 1673 by Wikipedia and MacTutor; the day is not given in the reachable sources.
stops.campa: He goes up to The Queen's College in July, seventeen years old, carrying telescopes and a sextant his father paid for. Undergraduates at Oxford do not usually own instruments. He is already setting the printed tables of planetary positions against what he can see for himself, and finding that the tables are wrong, which is a thing an undergraduate is not usually placed to know. He will leave without a degree. Oxford will give him one anyway, by order of the king, five years from now.
suggested_refs: The buttery books and admission registers of The Queen's College, Oxford, 1673
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Edmond Halley

stops.name: Greenwich, the letters to the Astronomer Royal
stops.date_confidence: MacTutor dates the correspondence with Flamsteed and the assistance at Greenwich to 1675 and gives no month; month and day default to 01 January. The Royal Observatory was founded in the same year. The pool's chronology lens listed this entry after the 1676 occultation; the dates order it here.
stops.campa: In the year the king puts an observatory on the hill above Greenwich to fix the longitude for his navy, an eighteen-year-old undergraduate writes to its first occupant about errors in the astronomical tables, and is taken seriously enough to be set to work at the instruments. John Flamsteed is twenty-nine and beginning a catalogue of the northern sky that will take him forty years and that he will guard like money. Forty-five years from now Halley will hold this post himself, and the manner of his coming to it will not be forgiven.
suggested_refs: Flamsteed's early Greenwich observation books, 1675-1676
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Edmond Halley

stops.name: Oxford, the Moon passes over Mars
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, 11 June 1676, by MacTutor.
stops.campa: On the eleventh of June the Moon moves across the face of Mars and puts it out. He times the occultation and writes it up, and the Philosophical Transactions print it: a first publication by a student who has not graduated and will not. An occultation is a clock. Knowing to the second when one body covers another gives you the distance between the two places on the ground that watched it happen, and the whole problem of longitude is a problem of clocks. He is nineteen and has found the instrument he will use for sixty years.
suggested_refs: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society, Halley's account of the occultation of Mars, 1676
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Edmond Halley

stops.name: Saint Helena, the observatory in the cloud
stops.date_confidence: he sailed in November 1676, attested by Wikipedia and MacTutor; the date of landfall is not given, and the stop is dated to the sailing. MacTutor's 'roughly eighteen months there' cannot be fitted between the November 1676 sailing and the May 1678 return along with two ocean passages; the contradiction is recorded and not resolved.
stops.campa: He leaves Oxford without a degree and takes ship for the loneliest inhabited rock in the Atlantic, backed by Charles II and the East India Company, to write down the stars nobody in Europe can see. He builds an observatory on the island and works through cloud that comes off the sea and does not lift. He fixes the positions of 341 southern stars and notes a cluster in Centaurus. Ptolemy's catalogue and every catalogue after it had a hole in it the size of half the sky, and a man of twenty goes out and fills it.
suggested_refs: The site of Halley's observatory on Saint Helena, on the ridge now called Halley's Mount
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Edmond Halley

stops.name: Saint Helena, the transit of Mercury
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, 7 November 1677, by MacTutor.
stops.campa: On the seventh of November the planet Mercury crosses the disc of the Sun, and he watches the whole passage through a telescope from first contact to last: the first complete telescopic observation of such a transit anyone has made. A small black dot walks across a fire. He notes how sharply the moments of contact can be timed, and that two observers far apart would time them differently, and that the difference between them is a measurement of something. He is twenty-one. He will publish what to do with it thirty-nine years from now.
suggested_refs: Halley's report of the 1677 transit of Mercury, Philosophical Transactions
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Edmond Halley

stops.name: Gresham College, the return and the fellowship
stops.date_confidence: Wikipedia attests the election to 30 November 1678, the Society's anniversary day, and MacTutor gives a similar date. The return from Saint Helena is attested to May 1678 without a day. The nickname Southern Tycho is attested in DNB and in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, both of which give it to him for the southern catalogue; DNB credits the coinage to Flamsteed without naming the document in which Flamsteed used it, so the attribution is reported rather than documented. Pin inherited from newton.journey.json, which places the Royal Society at Gresham College from 1673.
stops.campa: He lands in England in May with the southern sky in a notebook, and on the anniversary day in November the Royal Society elects him Fellow. He is twenty-two, one of the youngest ever taken in. Flamsteed, whose own catalogue of the northern stars is three years begun and nowhere near finished, calls him the Southern Tycho. It is said in praise and remembered as praise. Thirty-four years from now the same man will call him a lazy and malicious thief, over the same kind of catalogue, and mean every word.
suggested_refs: The Royal Society Journal Book for 30 November 1678
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Edmond Halley

stops.name: Oxford, the degree by royal command
stops.date_confidence: attested to 3 December 1678 by Wikipedia.
stops.campa: Three days after the Royal Society takes him in, a letter from Charles II instructs Oxford to give the man a Master of Arts without examination. He never sat the schools, never finished the course, and walks out of the university a master on the strength of a rock in the South Atlantic and 341 stars. The king's word does in an afternoon what four years of residence does for everybody else. Thirteen years from now the same university will refuse him a chair, and no letter from a king will come.
suggested_refs: The royal mandate of 3 December 1678 in the Oxford University registers

stops.name: London, Catalogus Stellarum Australium
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1679 by Wikipedia and MacTutor; month and day are not in the reachable sources and default to 01 January. The catalogue itself was not consulted; the figure of 341 stars rests on Wikipedia and MacTutor agreeing.
stops.campa: The catalogue is printed: 341 stars of the southern hemisphere, their positions fixed by a young man alone on an island with instruments he owned himself. It is the first such catalogue made with a telescope, and it closes the half of the sky that Tycho Brahe at Uraniborg and Johannes Hevelius at Danzig had to leave open because neither of them had ever been south of the line. Europe now holds a whole sky on paper. The man who supplied the missing half is twenty-three and has no degree he earned.
suggested_refs: Catalogus Stellarum Australium, London, 1679
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Edmond Halley

stops.name: Danzig, the referee sent to Hevelius
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1679 by Wikipedia; no month is given in the reachable sources, and May is a sort placeholder inside the year rather than a claim.
stops.campa: The Royal Society sends him to Danzig to settle a quarrel. Robert Hooke says that Johannes Hevelius, who refuses telescopic sights and measures the stars with open sights and his naked eye, cannot possibly be as accurate as he claims. Halley, twenty-two, arrives to audit a man of sixty-eight inside his own observatory. He observes beside him for weeks and reports that the old method holds, that the eye is as good as the lenses. The verdict costs Halley nothing and costs Hooke a little, and Hevelius dies vindicated.
suggested_refs: Hevelius's observatory on Korzenna Street, Danzig, and his Machina Coelestis

stops.name: Paris, the comet at Calais and Cassini's table
stops.date_confidence: MacTutor dates the tour to 1680, with the comet observed near Calais and work with Cassini in Paris, and says he spent much of the following year in Italy. December 1680 is the month of the great comet's appearance and is used as the sort key. No Italian city is named in any reachable source, so the Italian year of 1681 gets no stop; the itinerary has a hole in it and the hole is left open.
stops.campa: Crossing to France he sees the great comet of 1680 from near Calais, and carries the sighting on to the Paris Observatory, where Giovanni Domenico Cassini sets him computing its path. Cassini floats the idea that the thing might be periodic, a body on a long return rather than a portent passing once. Halley does not take it up yet. Newton will use this same comet, seven years from now, to demonstrate the law of gravitation in a book Halley pays to print, and it will end up carved on a marble globe above Newton's tomb.
suggested_refs: Cassini's observations of the comet of 1680 at the Observatoire de Paris
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Edmond Halley

stops.name: Islington, the marriage and the comet
stops.date_confidence: the marriage to Mary Tooke is attested to 1682 by Wikipedia and MacTutor without month or day; the comet observation is attested to September 1682 by MacTutor. The stop carries the September date and the marriage sits inside the same year. Nothing else about Mary Tooke is in the reachable sources: no death date, no names for the three children.
stops.campa: He marries Mary Tooke and they take a house at Islington, north of the city, where they will live and raise three children. In September of the same year a comet comes up over the roofs, and he watches it as everybody in England watches it, and writes down where it stands against the stars night after night. He is twenty-five and it means nothing in particular to him yet. Twenty-three years from now he will work out that this one is a returning visitor, and it will take his name.
suggested_refs: Halley's Islington house and his 1682 observations of the comet
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Edmond Halley

stops.name: Gresham College, Kepler's third law and the news from home
stops.date_confidence: the Royal Society presentation is attested to 24 January 1684 by MacTutor. The father's disappearance is attested to March 1684 with the body found roughly five weeks later, circumstances never resolved; nothing else about it is in the reachable sources. The pool's chronology lens listed the January presentation after the August visit to Cambridge; the dates order them here.
stops.campa: In January he lays before the Society what he has got out of Kepler's third law: that the force holding a planet in its orbit must fall off as the square of the distance. Hooke says he has had it for years and will not show his proof. Christopher Wren offers a book worth forty shillings to whoever produces one. In March his father walks out of the house and does not come back, and is found dead five weeks later, and nobody ever establishes how. He is twenty-seven, head of a damaged estate, holding an unproved theorem.
suggested_refs: The Royal Society Journal Book for 24 January 1684
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Edmond Halley

stops.name: Trinity College, Halley's question
stops.date_confidence: attested to August 1684 by De Moivre's account as recorded by Conduitt; the day is not given. Pin and date inherited byte for byte from newton.journey.json, which carries this same scene from the other side.
stops.campa: He rides to Cambridge to ask a recluse the question nobody in London can answer: what curve would a planet describe, if it were drawn by a force falling off as the square of the distance. Newton says at once, an ellipse. Asked how he knows, he says he has calculated it. He cannot find the paper. He promises to send it on. What arrives is nine pages, and then a book, and Halley spends three years making sure the book exists. One man had the proof in a drawer. The other man went and asked for it.
stops.quote: For when he had obtained of me my demonstrations of the figure of the celestial orbits, he continually pressed me to communicate the same to the Royal Society
stops.quote_source: Isaac Newton, Author's Preface to Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica, 1729 Motte translation, Wikisource
suggested_refs: De motu corporum in gyrum, the nine-page tract Newton sent after the visit, Royal Society register 1684
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Edmond Halley

stops.name: Gresham College, the clerkship and the chart of the winds
stops.date_confidence: the clerkship of the Philosophical Transactions is attested to 1685 by MacTutor and the wind chart to 1686 by Wikipedia and MacTutor; neither carries a month. The stop is dated 1686 and holds both, with month and day defaulting to 01 January.
stops.campa: He takes the Society's clerkship and edits the Philosophical Transactions, a salaried job for a man whose inheritance did not survive his father. In the same span he draws a map of the world with the trade winds on it: arrows across the oceans showing which way the air moves and where the belts of calm lie, compiled out of sailors' reports and out of what he saw himself between England and Saint Helena. Nobody has mapped a fluid before. The first weather chart ever drawn is an instrument for getting a ship across an ocean.
suggested_refs: Halley's 1686 chart of the trade winds and monsoons, Philosophical Transactions
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Edmond Halley

stops.name: London, Streater's press
stops.date_confidence: July 1687 is attested; the day is not. Pin and date inherited from newton.journey.json, which notes that the 5 July in circulation appears to come from confusion with the licensing a year earlier.
stops.campa: The Royal Society votes to print the manuscript and then discovers it has spent its printing money on a history of fishes. Halley pays for the Principia himself, out of a clerk's salary. He edits it, corrects the proofs, takes care of the diagrams, and talks Newton out of suppressing the third book when Hooke claims the inverse-square law as his own. Joseph Streater prints five hundred copies. Halley's name appears in the volume once, on a Latin ode at the front, and Newton says the rest in the preface.
stops.quote: In the publication of this Work, the most acute and universally learned Mr. Edmund Halley not only assisted me with his pains in correcting the press and taking care of the schemes, but it was to his solicitations that its becoming publick is owing.
stops.quote_source: Isaac Newton, Author's Preface to Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica, 1729 Motte translation, Wikisource
suggested_refs: The first edition of the Principia, London, 1687, with Halley's prefatory ode
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Edmond Halley
Royal Society Council minutes, 1686, cited through newton.journey.json

segments.name: The Chair Refused and the Shells Within

stops.name: Oxford, the chair refused
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1691 by Wikipedia and MacTutor; month and day are not in the reachable sources and default to 01 January. Flamsteed's part in the opposition is reported rather than documented in anything reachable.
stops.campa: The Savilian Chair of Astronomy falls vacant and he stands for it. John Tillotson, Archbishop of Canterbury, and Bishop Stillingfleet oppose him on the ground that he doubts the Earth is as young as Genesis says it is, and Flamsteed is reported to have worked against him as well. The chair goes to David Gregory. The man who filled in half the sky is judged unsound on the age of the ground under his feet. The objection is never answered; it is outlived. Oxford takes him only once the objectors are dead.
suggested_refs: The Savilian Chair of Astronomy election of 1691 and David Gregory's appointment
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Edmond Halley

stops.name: London, the diving bell
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1691 by Wikipedia; no month is given and June is a sort placeholder inside the year. The pool names no location for the trials, so the stop is pinned to London by default rather than by evidence.
stops.campa: Refused the chair, he builds a bell. Wood weighted with lead, open at the bottom, the air inside renewed from barrels lowered on a line and the stale air vented off through a tap, so that men can work on the seabed for an hour and a half instead of the length of one breath. He goes down in it himself. In the same year he is working on the design of marine compasses. The astronomer who could not get a professorship spends the year under water and over a needle, on the two instruments a ship cannot sail without.
suggested_refs: Halley's account of his diving bell in the Philosophical Transactions

stops.name: Gresham College, the shells within the Earth
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1692 as a Philosophical Transactions paper, summarised by Wikipedia; month and day default to 01 January. The paper itself could not be read: royalsocietypublishing.org returned HTTP 403, archive.org was rate-limited or returned 404, and Wikisource does not hold it. The 500-mile figure and the two-shells-plus-core structure therefore rest on modern secondary paraphrase alone, and the only period wording reachable is DNB's, which quotes just two words of Halley.
stops.campa: The compass needle will not stay put. Its declination changes from place to place and from year to year, and no single fixed magnet in the ground accounts for that. So he proposes moving ones. The Earth is a shell some five hundred miles thick, and inside it two more shells and a solid core, each turning at its own rate, each carrying its own poles, separated by luminous atmospheres. The inner spaces are lit, and may be inhabited, and the gas escaping from them is the aurora. Athanasius Kircher had hollowed the earth out with fire-channels twenty-seven years earlier.
stops.quote: He supposed auroræ to be occasioned by the escape of a 'luminous medium,' by which a subterranean globe was rendered habitable.
stops.quote_source: Dictionary of National Biography, 1885-1900, 'Halley, Edmund'. Only the two words in inner quotation marks are Halley's; the sentence around them is the DNB author's paraphrase.
suggested_refs: Halley, 'An Account of the Cause of the Change of the Variation of the Magnetical Needle', Philosophical Transactions, 1692

stops.name: Gresham College, the Breslau tables
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1693 by Wikipedia and MacTutor; month and day are not in the reachable sources and default to 01 January. Halley never went to Breslau; the stop is pinned to London, where the work was done on another city's registers.
stops.campa: A clergyman in Silesia has kept the registers of Breslau, births and deaths by age, for a city with little migration either way, and the numbers reach London. Halley works them into a table showing how many of a thousand people born are still alive at every age up to eighty-four. Then he does the thing nobody has done: he prices an annuity off it. What a life is worth to buy, at a given age, in money. Governments have been selling annuities at one rate to all comers. The astronomer who never saw Breslau has told them what each buyer is worth.
suggested_refs: Halley's 1693 Breslau life table, Philosophical Transactions
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Edmond Halley

stops.name: Gresham College, the comet that drowned the world
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1694 by Wikipedia; month and day are not given and default to 01 January. The papers were judged too controversial and were not printed until 1724, eighteen years before his death and thirty after the reading.
stops.campa: He tells the Society that the biblical Flood was a comet strike: a body came in, tipped the world, and the water went over everything. The Society finds it too dangerous to print and sits on the papers for thirty years. John Cleves Symmes will spend the 1820s petitioning Congress for ships to find the entrance to the inner spheres, and Leonhard Euler will be blamed for an inner sun he never proposed. Halley built the shells to explain a compass needle. They are remembered as a fantasy about a hollow world.
suggested_refs: Halley's papers on the Flood, read 1694, printed in the Philosophical Transactions in 1724

stops.name: Chester, deputy comptroller of the Mint
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1696 by Wikipedia and MacTutor, the post held about two years; month and day are not in the reachable sources and default to 01 January.
stops.campa: Newton, made Warden of the Mint, gets him the deputy comptrollership of the Chester branch, one of the country mints opened to take in the clipped silver of England and strike it again. He counts coin for two years in a provincial castle while the currency of a kingdom is remade around him. The debt has turned around: the man who paid for the Principia now draws a salary from the man who wrote it. Neither of them is doing astronomy. Both of them are working on money.
suggested_refs: The Chester branch mint in Chester Castle during the great recoinage, 1696-1698
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Edmond Halley

stops.name: Deptford, the Tsar and the commission
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1698 by Wikipedia, the meeting dated to Peter the Great's English visit of that year with no day given, so month and day default to 01 January. The content of the conversation, shipbuilding and science, is reported rather than documented.
stops.campa: Peter the Great comes to England to learn shipbuilding, takes John Evelyn's house at Deptford beside the yards, and ruins the garden. Halley is sent to talk to him, and they talk about ships and about the sciences a navy needs. In the same year the Admiralty gives Halley a command of his own: captain of the Paramour, a pink of some fifty feet, ordered into the Atlantic to measure how far the compass lies. The orders tell him to attempt the discovery of what land lies to the south of the western ocean.
stops.quote: attempt the discovery of what land lies to the south of the western ocean
stops.quote_source: The orders for the Paramour Pink voyage, quoted in the Dictionary of National Biography, 1885-1900, 'Halley, Edmund'
suggested_refs: Sayes Court, Deptford, and the Admiralty commission of the Paramour Pink, 1698

stops.name: The South Atlantic, the lieutenant
stops.date_confidence: attested to November 1698 by Wikipedia and MacTutor; no day is given and 20 November is a sort placeholder inside the month. The coordinate is a mid-Atlantic point standing for a track and is not a fix: the pool gives no positions for the outward leg and no port of departure or return for any of the three voyages.
stops.campa: A civilian in command of a king's ship, with a naval lieutenant under him who does not accept it. The lieutenant obstructs him, questions his seamanship in front of the crew, and the voyage that was to have run the length of the Atlantic turns back early. Halley brings the ship home and prefers charges, and the man is court-martialled. It is the first voyage the English navy ever fits out for no purpose but knowledge, and it fails on the oldest problem at sea, which is not the weather and is not the compass.
suggested_refs: The court martial of Halley's lieutenant, Admiralty records, 1699
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Edmond Halley

stops.name: Fifty-two degrees south, the islands of ice
stops.date_confidence: the second voyage sailed 24 August 1699 and ended 6 September 1700, both attested by Wikipedia and MacTutor; the southern limit is dated to the austral summer of early 1700 as a sort key and not as a fix. The coordinate is 52 degrees south, the latitude DNB attaches to Halley's account of the ice, on a longitude between the Falklands and South Georgia; the pool gives no position.
stops.campa: He is recommissioned and this time he goes south until the sea stops him. At fifty-two degrees he runs into islands of ice, and writes that he scarcely dares set down what he thinks about their height and their size. He turns north, coasts South America and then Africa taking compass readings the whole way, and is home on the sixth of September. Out of it comes the General Chart of the Variation, curved lines drawn across the oceans joining every place where the needle lies by the same amount.
stops.quote: fell in with great islands of ice, of so incredible a height and magnitude that I scarce dare write my thoughts of it
stops.quote_source: Halley's account of the Paramour Pink voyage, quoted in the Dictionary of National Biography, 1885-1900, 'Halley, Edmund'
suggested_refs: A General Chart of the Variation of the Compass, London, 1701, with the first published isogonic lines
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Edmond Halley

stops.name: The English Channel, the tides of the Paramour
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1701 by Wikipedia and MacTutor; no month is given and June is a sort placeholder inside the year. The coordinate is a point in the central Channel standing for a survey and is not a fix.
stops.campa: A third voyage in the same small ship, this time no further than the water between England and France, charting the tides and the coastline for the Admiralty. He records the times of high water along both shores and draws them, and the chart goes to the navy. Three commissions in three years, all of them survey work, all of them given to a man of forty-five with no sea training and a Master of Arts he did not sit for. The navy has found a use for a scholar and does not have a name for it.
suggested_refs: Halley's 1702 chart of the tides and coasts of the English Channel
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Edmond Halley

stops.name: Trieste, the Queen's harbours
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1702 by Wikipedia and MacTutor, which describe missions to the Adriatic and to Trieste for Queen Anne; no month is given and November is a sort placeholder inside the year. The pool does not say how many separate journeys there were.
stops.campa: Queen Anne sends him to the Adriatic to look at harbours: the imperial ports on the gulf, and whether they can be fortified for a war England is fighting over the Spanish succession. He measures moles and soundings and writes the reports himself. The Crown sends an astronomer for this because the answer has to be a number and the number has to be right the first time. He is forty-six, a Fellow of twenty-four years' standing, and has published nothing on the sky in years.
suggested_refs: Halley's reports to Queen Anne on the fortification of the Adriatic harbours, 1702-1703
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Edmond Halley

stops.name: Oxford, the chair at last
stops.date_confidence: Wikipedia dates the appointment to November 1703; MacTutor dates it 1704. The contradiction is recorded and not resolved, and the earlier date is used as the sort key.
stops.campa: John Wallis dies and Oxford gives Halley the Savilian Chair of Geometry, twelve years after refusing him the Chair of Astronomy over his opinions on the age of the world. His opinions have not changed in the twelve years. The men who objected to them are dead. He gives an inaugural lecture and it is well received, and he keeps the chair for the remaining thirty-nine years of his life, teaching geometry in the university that would not have him at thirty-four and takes him at forty-seven.
suggested_refs: The Savilian Chair of Geometry and Halley's inaugural lecture, Oxford, 1703
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Edmond Halley

stops.name: Oxford, Astronomiae Cometicae Synopsis
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1705 by Wikipedia and MacTutor; month and day are not in the reachable sources and default to 01 January. The pool's chronology lens names three apparitions, 1531, 1607 and 1682; its afterlife lens names four, adding 1456. Both derive from Wikipedia articles and they are not reconciled here. The Synopsis itself was not consulted.
stops.campa: He computes the orbits of two dozen comets out of every record he can find, and three of them come out the same: 1531, 1607, 1682, the same path, the same tilt, seventy-five or seventy-six years apart. Either three separate bodies happen to travel identical roads, or it is one body coming back. He says it is one body. He says when it will return, near the end of 1758, and he says he will not be alive to see it, and he asks that posterity remember an Englishman worked it out.
stops.quote: candid posterity to acknowledge that this was first discovered by an Englishman
stops.quote_source: Halley on his prediction of the comet's return, quoted in the Dictionary of National Biography, 1885-1900, 'Halley, Edmund'
suggested_refs: Astronomiae Cometicae Synopsis, Oxford, 1705
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Edmond Halley

stops.name: Oxford, Apollonius out of the Arabic
stops.date_confidence: the translation of Books V to VII is attested to 1706 and the complete Latin edition of the Conics with the honorary doctorate to 1710, both by Wikipedia; neither carries a month. The stop takes the earlier date and holds the later work inside it. The reconstruction of the lost Book VIII is attested by the pool's afterlife lens, also from Wikipedia.
stops.campa: Books five to seven of Apollonius on conic sections survive in no Greek manuscript. They exist only in Arabic, made in Baghdad in the ninth century out of a Greek text that is gone. The Savilian Professor of Geometry learns enough Arabic to get them out, prints the whole Conics in Latin in 1710, and writes the lost eighth book himself from the internal evidence of the other seven. Oxford gives him a doctorate. The curves he is restoring are the curves he has just told the world a comet travels on.
suggested_refs: Apollonii Pergaei Conicorum libri octo, Halley's Latin edition, Oxford, 1710

stops.name: Oxford, the stars that are not fixed
stops.date_confidence: the deduction is dated about 1710 and the publication to 1717 or 1718, MacTutor and Wikipedia differing on the publication year; the disagreement is recorded and not resolved. Month and day are not given and default to 01 January.
stops.campa: He sets Ptolemy's catalogue, made at Alexandria fifteen and a half centuries ago, beside the positions he can measure now, and three stars do not match. Sirius, Procyon and Arcturus have moved. Not the whole sky wheeling, which was known, but three individual stars crawling out of place against the rest of them. The fixed stars are not fixed. They are suns going somewhere at speeds and in directions of their own, and the sky is a thing in motion that only looks like a ceiling.
suggested_refs: Halley's paper on the proper motions of Sirius, Procyon and Arcturus, Philosophical Transactions, 1718
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Edmond Halley

stops.name: Gresham College, Flamsteed's catalogue printed against him
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1712 by Wikipedia; month and day are not in the reachable sources and default to 01 January. Flamsteed's letter to Arbuthnot quoted here is dated 29 March 1711, a year before the edition appeared, on first learning that Halley would edit it.
stops.campa: Flamsteed has been observing at Greenwich for thirty-seven years and will not publish until the catalogue is finished. It is printed anyway, and Halley is put in charge of the edition. He fills the gaps, corrects what he judges wrong, and sets a critical preface at the front of another man's life's work. The relationship never recovers. Flamsteed calls him a lazy and malicious thief, says the catalogue was very effectually spoiled, and had already written that the ill-usage dishonoured the queen and the nation.
stops.quote: the neglect of me, and the ill-usage I had met with, was a dishonour to the queen and the nation
stops.quote_source: John Flamsteed to John Arbuthnot, 29 March 1711, quoted in the Dictionary of National Biography, 1885-1900, 'Flamsteed, John'
suggested_refs: Historia Coelestis Britannica, the 1712 edition prepared by Halley against Flamsteed's wishes

stops.name: Gresham College, the transit of Venus and the measure of the system
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1716 by Wikipedia; month and day are not in the reachable sources and default to 01 January. The method was carried out in 1761 and 1769, nineteen and twenty-seven years after his death.
stops.campa: Kepler gave the proportions of the solar system, but nobody has its size: every orbit is known as a ratio to every other and the ruler is missing. Halley, sixty, writes out the method. When Venus crosses the Sun, observers stationed far apart on the Earth will see the crossing take different lengths of time; that difference gives the parallax, and the parallax gives the distance. The next transits fall in 1761 and 1769. He tells astronomers not yet born exactly what to do and where to stand, and asks them to go.
suggested_refs: Halley's 1716 paper on observing the transits of Venus, Philosophical Transactions

stops.name: Stonehenge, the stones dated
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1720 by Wikipedia; month and day are not in the reachable sources and default to 01 January. The pool gives no detail of the method beyond astronomical and antiquarian reasoning, and no figure for the date he arrived at.
stops.campa: He goes out onto Salisbury Plain and tries to put a year on a stone circle. The axis of the thing points at the midsummer sunrise, and the place where the sun comes up on the longest day creeps along the horizon over the centuries as the tilt of the Earth changes, so the alignment is a clock if the drift can be measured. It is among the earliest attempts anyone makes to date a prehistoric monument by something other than legend. The man refused a chair for doubting the age of the world is out dating the world's furniture.
suggested_refs: The early eighteenth-century antiquarian surveys of Stonehenge

stops.name: Greenwich, second Astronomer Royal
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1720, the year of Flamsteed's death, by Wikipedia and MacTutor; no month is given and month and day default to 01 January. The Saros programme of lunar observations is attested to 1721 and is carried in this stop. The quotation is from the Royal Society council of 2 March 1727, two days after Newton's last presiding appearance there.
stops.campa: Flamsteed dies and the post goes to the man who printed his catalogue against his will. He is sixty-four when he takes the Royal Observatory, forty-five years after writing to its first occupant as an undergraduate about errors in the tables. He sets himself one task and it is an eighteen-year task: to observe the Moon through a complete Saros, the cycle after which eclipses repeat, and get lunar tables good enough for a ship to find its longitude by. He finishes the cycle at eighty-two and keeps the results in his own hands.
stops.quote: had hitherto kept them in his own custody, that he might have time to finish the theory he designed to build upon them
stops.quote_source: Halley addressing the council of the Royal Society, 2 March 1727, quoted in the Dictionary of National Biography, 1885-1900, 'Halley, Edmund'
suggested_refs: Halley's Saros lunar observations at the Royal Observatory, 1722-1739
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Edmond Halley

stops.name: Greenwich, the death
stops.date_confidence: MacTutor gives 14 January 1742 Old Style; Wikipedia gives 25 January 1742 New Style. They are the same day in two calendars, and the sources lead with one or the other without always saying which. England did not adopt the Gregorian calendar until 1752, so the Old Style date is what Greenwich itself would have written, and it is used as the sort key; the file's calendar field reads gregorian because the life falls after 1582. Neither date is preferred as true.
stops.campa: He dies at Greenwich, eighty-five years old, second Astronomer Royal, in the twenty-second year of the post and observing to the end of it. The comet is sixteen years out from the return he named for it, somewhere out past the far end of its orbit and coming, and there is no way for anybody alive to know whether he was right. The Moon tables are finished and unpublished, held in his own custody, waiting on a theory he did not get the time to build on them. Newton has been dead fifteen years.
suggested_refs: The Royal Observatory, Greenwich, in Halley's occupancy, 1720-1742
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Edmond Halley

stops.name: Lee, the grave at St Margaret's
stops.date_confidence: the burial is attested to 1742 by Wikipedia without month or day, so month and day default to 01 January by the file convention, which places this stop before the death date in sort order. The old church was later rebuilt and a marked grave identifying Halley remains in the churchyard; the pool does not date the rebuilding.
stops.campa: He is buried in the churchyard of the old St Margaret's at Lee, in Blackheath, in a vault that will afterwards take John Pond, another Astronomer Royal. Nathaniel Bliss, another again, lies nearby in the same ground in an unmarked grave. Three men who ran the same observatory end in one small churchyard on the south side of the river. The church around them is pulled down and built again, and the grave keeps its marker through the rebuilding, which is more than the vault's other occupants manage.
suggested_refs: The churchyard of old St Margaret's, Lee Terrace, Blackheath, and the Halley vault

stops.name: Royal Observatory, Greenwich: the stone on the Camera Obscura wall
stops.date_confidence: undated in the pool. Wikipedia attests that the British Admiralty relocated the original tombstone to the southern wall of the Camera Obscura building at the Royal Observatory and gives no year. 1742-01-01 is a sort placeholder keeping the stop beside the burial, and is not a claim about when the stone was moved.
stops.campa: The Admiralty takes his tombstone off the grave at Lee and mounts it on the south wall of the Camera Obscura at the Royal Observatory, half an hour's walk from the body it was cut for. The stone stands at Greenwich, where he worked for twenty-two years and tracked the Moon through a whole Saros. The man lies in a Blackheath churchyard, in a vault he shares with a later Astronomer Royal. Neither place holds both. It is a navy that does this, to a man the navy commissioned three times and sent to fifty-two degrees south in a ship of fifty feet.
suggested_refs: Halley's original tombstone on the south wall of the Camera Obscura, Royal Observatory Greenwich

stops.name: Westminster Abbey, the comet in the South Cloister
stops.date_confidence: undated in the pool. Wikipedia attests a comet-shaped plaque commemorating Halley in the South Cloister of Westminster Abbey and gives no year. 1742-01-01 is a sort placeholder and not a claim. Pin inherited byte for byte from newton.journey.json and lord_kelvin.journey.json.
stops.campa: A plaque cut in the shape of a comet goes up in the South Cloister. Newton is already fifteen years in the nave, under a marble globe with the path of the comet of 1680 traced across it, the comet Halley computed at Cassini's table as a young man. Lord Kelvin will be laid down just south of Newton in 1907. The Abbey gathers the Royal Society's dead into one floor, and the man who paid for the Principia out of a clerk's wages gets the cloister, and gets the comet.
suggested_refs: The comet-shaped memorial to Halley in the South Cloister, Westminster Abbey

stops.name: Near Dresden, the farmer who sees it first
stops.date_confidence: attested to 25 December 1758 by Wikipedia. The perihelion of that return fell on 13 March 1759, close to the date Alexis Clairaut had computed after allowing for the perturbations of Jupiter and Saturn; that second date is carried in this stop rather than given a pin of its own.
stops.campa: On Christmas night a farmer outside Dresden who grinds his own lenses points a telescope at the sky and finds a comet where Halley said one would be. Johann Georg Palitzsch holds no post and draws no salary. Alexis Clairaut in Paris has spent months computing how far Jupiter and Saturn will drag the thing off schedule, and has named a date; perihelion comes on the thirteenth of March, near enough. A dead man's arithmetic is checked against the sky and it holds. The comet takes his name.
suggested_refs: Palitzsch's house and observatory at Prohlis, near Dresden

stops.name: Florida, Missouri: the comet's fortnight
stops.date_confidence: the perihelion of 16 November 1835 is attested. mark_twain.journey.json carries this same event pinned to 1835-11-30, the date of the birth a fortnight later; this stop carries the perihelion date instead, so the two files hold two dates for one pin. Pin inherited byte for byte from mark_twain.journey.json, whose own note records that the pool's coordinate for Florida, Missouri was wrong twice over.
stops.campa: The comet comes to perihelion on the sixteenth of November. Two weeks later, in a hamlet of a hundred people in Monroe County, Missouri, Jane Lampton Clemens bears a sixth child two months early and he is named Samuel Langhorne. Seventy-four years on he will write down that he came in with the comet and expects to go out with it. Halley computed a period of seventy-five or seventy-six years for the object. A man can be born under it and die under it, and one will.
suggested_refs: The frame house at Florida, Missouri, now within the Mark Twain Birthplace State Historic Site

stops.name: Stormfield, Redding: the appointment kept
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the perihelion of that return fell on 20 April 1910. Pin and date inherited byte for byte from mark_twain.journey.json.
stops.campa: The comet reaches perihelion on the twentieth of April. On the twenty-first, at Stormfield in Connecticut, Samuel Clemens dies of a heart attack, one day behind it, having set the arrangement down in a dictation the year before. The newspapers print the prediction alongside the obituary. An orbit worked out at Oxford in 1705 by a man who asked posterity to remember an Englishman did it has now been used twice, to time the entrance and the exit of an American.
stops.quote: I came in with Halley's comet in 1835. It is coming again next year, and I expect to go out with it.
stops.quote_source: Mark Twain, autobiographical dictation of 1909, quoted in Wikipedia, 'Mark Twain'
suggested_refs: Stormfield, Redding, Connecticut, and Twain's 1909 autobiographical dictation

stops.name: Halley Research Station, the names given after
stops.date_confidence: the date is Giotto's flyby of the comet's nucleus, 14 March 1986, the only date the pool attaches to this cluster of posthumous namings. The founding date of the Antarctic station is not in the pool, and the roads, streets and craters carrying his name are undated there too. The comet's next return is given as 28 July 2061.
stops.campa: A British research station stands on an ice shelf at seventy-five degrees south, below the latitude where he met the icebergs, and it is called Halley. There is a road at the Oxford Science Park, a way on the Greenwich Peninsula, a drive in Virginia, a street in Avignon, a crater on the Moon and a crater on Mars. On the fourteenth of March 1986 a European probe named Giotto passes nearer to the nucleus of the comet than anything has, and photographs it. The comet is due again on the twenty-eighth of July 2061.
suggested_refs: Halley Research Station on the Brunt Ice Shelf; the Giotto images of the comet's nucleus, March 1986
